# Can Artificial Intelligence maintain and debug complex code bases autonomously?

The video discusses whether AI agents can find and fix bugs alone on large code bases. It features the SWE-sweep, where the agent receives entire repositories without any hints, fault tracking and fuzzing techniques, high cost and low rate of hit, and the risk of double use in cybersecurity.

Video by Maurício Yokoyama Issei, published on October 17, 2026 (7 min 34 s).
Watch: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5rzZYy5JODM

_The video and the transcript are in Portuguese. The minutes between brackets, such as [04:12], point to the excerpt of the video._

## Finding the bug is the neck

The video asks if the AI can find and fix bugs without human help. Solving an isolated problem is very different from receiving a huge code base and finding out for yourself what is broken [00:42].

A 2018 article summarizes the question: you cannot fix what is not found. Applying the repair is usually the easy part; the hard part is to locate the line that causes the problem [01:03].

This stage is called fault location and is the first step of any autonomous system [01:24].

Recent searches attack this problem: LLMAO tries to find errors without running tests, and AgentFL expands the search for the entire project [01:44].

According to the video, the AgentFL navigates the code and confirms hypotheses, as a person would, and locates the failure in 97 seconds, at a cost of 7 cents [02:06].

## From guided to autonomous

In SWE-bench, the AI received a description of the problem, with tips on what to do [02:26].

In SWE-sweep, the agent enters 100 repositories with over 4,000 bugs without any hints and needs to figure out what to fix by itself [02:47].

The evaluation uses Harbor, an isolated testing environment. The cycle restores the original repository, applies the agent code, compiles if applicable and runs the tests. If the agent fixes something, but breaks what already worked, the grade is zero [03:08].

## How to equip the agent

People use mouse and windows; AI also needs its own interface. SWE-agent search calls this ACI, agent-computer interface: tools that let the model read long texts, create files and use the terminal without getting lost [03:51].

Another technique is fuzzing: send random data to the software to see if it breaks [03:51].

According to the video, TitanFuzz uses code-trained language models to generate tests that respect language rules. He found unpublished bugs in large AI libraries and increased code coverage by almost 51% compared to traditional methods [04:12].

## The cost of debugging per AI

According to the video, the highest success rate in the SWE-sweep ranking to fix bugs without any hint was 4.7%, from the Sol 5.6 model [04:35]. On the project page, updated on November 2, 2026, the best ranking result is already another, with 8.9%.

The result shows that pure autonomy is still at the beginning. This model costs more than US$ 72 per tested repository [04:58]. Cheaper models, such as Luna 5.6, do not reach 3% success [05:20].

Giving more processing time does not solve: there are decreasing yields. Running free for a long time, the agent often undoes useful repairs he himself had made [05:41].

## The cybersecurity border

If the AI is good at searching systems for bugs, it can also use this to attack. Cybench measures this risk: tests models like GPT-4o and Claude 3.5 Sonnet with real competition challenges Capture the Flag [06:02].

According to the video, AI agents find the breach and invade in minutes, while the best human teams take hours [06:23]. In the most difficult cases, almost 25 hours [06:44].

It is the problem of double use: the same AI that can patrol a software and close loopholes can also invade it faster than a person accompanies. The question remains who will find the flaw first, who defends or who attacks [07:05].

## Frequently Asked Questions

### What's the difference between SWE-bench and SWE-sweep?

In SWE-bench, the agent gets a description of the problem. In SWE-sweep, you get the entire repository, no hints, and you need to find the bugs yourself [02:47].

### Why does a regression zero the grade?

Because the goal is to fix it without breaking what already worked. If the correction breaks a passing test, the note of the task is zero [03:08].

## Fonts

- [SWE-sweep](https://swesweep.com): The SWE-sweep has 100 repositories and about 4.1 thousand bugs; agents receive no hints about the type or location of the bug, and a regression in the original test suite zeros the note. On November 2, 2026, the best ranking result was 8.9%.
- [facebookresearch/swe-sweep: How many bugs can LMs find & fix in large codebases?](https://github.com/facebookresearch/swe-sweep): The agent needs to figure out and fix as many bugs as possible in a real repository, and the project is a thin layer on Harbor, which runs the evaluation.

## About the video

In this video, we explore the **SWE-sweep**, a benchmark developed by researchers from Meta FAIR, Harvard University, University of Washington and Stanford University. While traditional benchmarks like the **SWE-bench** evaluate models providing a clear description of the problem to be solved, SWE-sweep puts AI agents in an open world scenario: they receive an entire code base containing multiple bugs and must **discover and fix as many failures as possible without any tips or previous reports**.

**Video Highlights:**
* **The SWE-sweep Challenge:** Assessment **100 open-source repositories** covering **22 programming languages** and a total of **4.068 bugs**.
* **How Evaluation Works:** The agent needs to navigate the code, identify deviations from expected behavior and apply corrections without breaking pre-existing tests (no regressions).
* **Tip Model Performance:** Even the model with the best result (GPT-5.6 Sun with mini-SWE-agent) solved only **4.7% of all bugs**.
* **The AI Gargalo:** The study reveals that the greatest difficulty of the agents is not in the writing of the correction code, but in the **location and autonomous discovery of defects**.
